subtype: Approach: negotiating a win-win with parents [Action]
passage: On Saturday night Nilesh laid a printed sheet on the table: fees for both colleges, entrance dates in April, average job outcomes for each path. “Ma, Papa, I'll appear for the engineering exam. In the evenings I'll also build a design portfolio, six pieces by December. If my rank is good and the portfolio is weak, I choose engineering. If it's the other way round, we sit down and talk again.” His mother, Nirmala, pushed her glasses up and read the sheet twice. “You're not just saying you don't want engineering?” “No, Ma. I'm giving both a fair chance.” Papa asked how he would learn design. “A free online course to begin with.” Papa nodded slowly. “Six pieces by December. We'll look at them together.”

qa.q: By when does Nilesh plan to have six design pieces?
What might Nilesh be worried about while presenting the sheet?
qa.a: That his parents will hear it as a rejection of engineering, so he shows that both paths get a fair chance.

qa.q: What else could Nilesh do to strengthen the deal, and why?
qa.a: Ask a working designer and an engineer to comment on his plan and portfolio, because outside views help his parents trust the arrangement.

qa.q: How does the proposal look to Nirmala?
qa.a: Nirmala sees facts and a deadline, and that her son's idea keeps engineering open, so she may feel reassured that he is not simply refusing.

grounding: A student prepares facts and proposes a plan that honours both his parents' view and his own interest.

"Papa, before you say anything, can I show you what I found?" Sachin put a folder on the dining table.

"Is this about design again?"

"Partly. Look." Sachin opened it. "Engineering entrance: forms close in January, exam in April. Fees at the state college: here. Placement data: here. I'll sit for it. I'm not refusing."

Papa's eyebrows went up. "Then what's the rest?"

"Design colleges take a portfolio and their own test in February. So while I prepare for engineering, I'll build a portfolio on weekends. Four hours on Sunday. If I get into both, we decide together, with the fees and job numbers in front of us."

His friend Ujjwal, who had come to study, sat very still on the sofa.

Papa read the page twice. "You've thought about this more than I have," he said finally. "All right. Both."

qa.q: How many hours on Sunday did Sachin plan for the portfolio?
How might Sachin have felt when Papa asked "Is this about design again?"
qa.a: Sachin was probably nervous, expecting a refusal, but prepared with facts.

qa.q: What else could Sachin do to keep the plan fair to both sides?
qa.a: Sachin could share progress on both the entrance preparation and the portfolio each month, so Papa sees neither is being neglected.

qa.q: How might Papa see Sachin's proposal?
qa.a: Papa seems impressed and persuaded, admitting Sachin has thought it through more than he has and agreeing to both.

grounding: Shows a student preparing facts on fees, entrance dates and job outcomes and proposing to parents to sit the engineering exam while building a design portfolio.

subtype: Approach: negotiating a win-win with parents [Action]
passage:
Two years ago my parents had one plan for me: engineering, like my father. I'd wanted architecture since I was twelve. I'm Tarun, and for months we just argued in circles.

My friend Mridul said, "Stop arguing. Bring them facts."

So I spent two weekends researching. I printed the entrance dates for both: the engineering entrance in April, the architecture aptitude test in May. Fees at our state colleges for both. The number of graduates who got jobs within a year, from each college's own report.

Then I made a proposal. I would prepare for and sit the engineering exam, fully. At the same time, I'd build an architecture portfolio on Saturdays and take the aptitude test in May. When results came, we'd choose together, with the numbers.

My father read it at the dining table for a long time. Then he said, "You've done my homework for me."

qa.q: When was the architecture aptitude test?
How did Tarun feel during the months of arguing?
qa.a: Tarun felt frustrated and stuck, going around in circles with the parents.

qa.q: What else could Tarun have included in the proposal?
qa.a: Tarun could have asked a practising architect to talk to the parents, so they hear about the career from someone in it.

qa.q: How might Tarun's father see the proposal?
qa.a: He seems impressed and a little humbled, saying Tarun had done his homework for him.

grounding: A reflective account of a student preparing facts on fees, entrance dates and job outcomes and proposing to sit the engineering exam while building a design portfolio.
